**MEMO: Compute Capacity — Buy More Hardware or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Local AI capacity planning for the next two quarters

We've reached the point where our GPU fleet is running hot enough that the question of capacity can no longer be deferred. Utilization on our primary inference nodes has averaged above 80 percent during business hours for six weeks, batch jobs are queuing overnight, and we've had two incidents where latency-sensitive workloads degraded because a training run was holding the cluster hostage. The instinctive response is to buy more hardware, and I want to explain why I think that instinct is half right, and why the other half matters more.

The case for buying is straightforward. Our current fleet was sized for a workload that has roughly tripled, and there's a real ceiling approaching. When we hit it, the failure mode isn't graceful — it's p99 latency blowing out, experiments stalling, and engineers quietly working around the queue in ways that make utilization data meaningless. Hardware lead times are also nontrivial; if we wait until we're desperate, we'll be paying spot-market prices and waiting eight weeks for delivery. Buying now, while we still have headroom, is cheaper than buying later under duress.

But the case for improving utilization is stronger than it first appears, and it's the part we've underinvested in. Our measured utilization of 80 percent overstates how much of that capacity is doing useful work. A meaningful fraction goes to idle-but-reserved memory from jobs that finished hours ago, to models held resident "just in case," and to batch work scheduled at times that collide with interactive demand. We have never built proper scheduling. Every team grabs the biggest node available because there's no mechanism to match job size to hardware, and no accountability for how long a reservation persists. Fixing this is not glamorous, but it's the difference between an 80 percent utilized cluster and a genuinely 80 percent *useful* one — and the gap between those two numbers is probably worth more than one new node.

Now the tradeoffs. Cost is the obvious axis: a new node is a capital expense plus power, cooling, and someone's time to integrate it, whereas scheduler work is a few engineer-weeks of existing headcount. Latency cuts both ways. Better scheduling means interactive jobs get priority and predictable response times, which is a direct improvement; a bigger fleet also improves latency, but only if the new capacity is actually free when someone needs it, which brings us back to scheduling. On reliability, more hardware gives us redundancy we currently lack — a single node failure today takes out a third of our inference capacity, which is a risk we've been lucky on so far. That argument for buying is real and I don't want to dismiss it.

The two considerations that tip me, though, are opportunity cost and reversibility. The opportunity cost of buying is that the same budget could fund the scheduling and observability work that makes *every* node we own, including any future ones, more productive. If we buy hardware first, we'll still need that work eventually, and we'll have paid for the node to avoid doing it. The reversibility point is subtler: hardware is a one-way door. Once purchased, it depreciates whether or not the demand materializes, and if our workload shifts — say, toward smaller models or a provider API for batch work — we're stuck with sunk capital. Scheduler improvements are a two-way door. If we build them and discover demand was real all along, we've lost a few weeks and gained permanent operational capability. If we buy first and demand was softer than it looked, we've lost real money.

So my recommendation is: fund the utilization work now, with a hard commitment to revisit hardware in eight weeks against measured numbers. Specifically, we should build job-level accounting, enforce reservation expiry, and implement basic priority scheduling. If, after that work, sustained useful utilization still exceeds roughly 70 percent with queuing on interactive workloads, we buy — and we'll then have the data to size the purchase correctly rather than guessing.

I want to be honest about the uncertainty here. My estimate of recoverable capacity is informed, not measured; it's possible the scheduler work yields only 10 percent and we end up buying anyway, having spent a quarter's delay on the answer. That's a risk I'm comfortable taking, because the alternative — buying on the strength of a utilization number we don't fully trust — is a larger bet on worse information. The eight-week checkpoint protects us either way.

Happy to discuss at Thursday's planning session.

appliance.hardware: 2 x NVIDIA DGX Spark, GB10, 128 GB unified memory per appliance
appliance.kv_cache_layout: MLA latent fp8_g128 (8448 B per 16-token block per layer, 11 layers) + sparse-index cache (1024 B per block per layer + slot-mapped tails); 2 GiB of it in the GB10 display carveout
appliance.serving_engine: Atlas (Enntity/atlas sparkglm/atlas-20261007-strings @ 7838b34c), image ghcr.io/enntity/atlas-sparkglm:6e2006864b70, SparkGLM 4x512k profile, GPU_MEMORY_UTILIZATION=0.91, display carveout on (latent pools only)
appliance.topology: TP2/EP2, direct ConnectX-7 RoCE link (RDMA pair)
